title: Area I review: Fundamentals of Instructing
intro: These questions mix the seven Tasks of Area I, the Fundamentals of Instructing: the learning process, human behavior and communication, the teaching process, teaching methods, critique and evaluation, instructor responsibilities, and planning. Most join two or more of them in one instrument training situation, such as a scenario flight that ends in a debrief, a stage check that tests a written objective, or an IPC that needs a plan and an honest logbook entry. The PTS has the evaluator select at least Tasks E, F and G and one other, so those three get a few more questions.

questions.q: On Tuesday your instrument learner flew the same ILS six times in a row, and each approach looked better than the last. On Friday's scenario flight, with a hold, a VOR approach and a missed approach mixed in, her ILS fell apart. What does the AIH say happened, and what do you change?
options: A learning plateau: tell her it is normal and temporary, then keep flying the same ILS each lesson until her scores climb again
Blocked practice: one repeated drill raised short-term scores but gave poorer long-term learning and fooled you both, so mix tasks in scenarios
Too little exercise: by the law of exercise six approaches were not enough, so fly twelve of the same ILS before the next scenario
Fading: three days without practice let the skill decay, so fly the same ILS drill on the morning of each scenario flight
questions.why: Blocked practice, the same drill until it becomes automatic, gives better short-term performance but poorer long-term learning, and it tends to fool both the learner and the instructor into thinking the skill is well learned [[25:78|AIH 3-27]]. Random practice mixes the skills through the session: it scores worse during practice but better on a test the next day, and well-written SBT encourages it [[25:78|AIH 3-27]]. A plateau is a leveling off after early gains, and the AIH's fix is to give the task a break, noting that over-practice can cause one [[25:77|AIH 3-26]]. Twelve of the same approach, or a warm-up drill of it, is still blocked practice and repeats the problem.

questions.q: Your school's two training airplanes have GPS navigators from different makers. In the same week your instrument learner starts on both, and now she mixes up the button sequences in each airplane. Which theory of forgetting fits, and what plan follows from it?
options: Positive transfer: the two units are alike, so keep alternating them every lesson, since practice on one speeds learning on the other
Repression: she is pushing the sequences out of mind to avoid anxiety, so talk about her fear of the avionics before going on
Fading: she has not used either unit long enough to keep it, so add time on both units each week until the sequences come back
Interference: similar material interferes most, and material not yet well learned suffers most, so teach one unit thoroughly first
questions.why: Interference theory says people forget because similar learning has intervened; similar material interferes with memory more than dissimilar material, and material not well learned suffers most [[25:89|AIH 3-38]]. Material thoroughly learned is highly resistant to forgetting [[25:89|AIH 3-38]], and the building block approach has the learner master blocks individually, then combine them [[25:146|AIH 7-2]]. When learning one skill hinders another, that is negative transfer, not positive [[25:91|AIH 3-40]], and because avionics formats are not standardized, moving from one maker's equipment to another should give a pilot pause [[25:22|AIH 1-18]]. Fading is about information not used for a long time [[25:89|AIH 3-38]], which is not her problem.

questions.q: Your instrument learner flies every approach to standard, but after lessons he jokes about 'taking a peek' below minimums on real trips and shrugs off your personal minimums worksheet. Which domain of learning holds the gap, and what does the AIH say about it?
options: The affective domain, his attitude toward safety and risk: standards are harder to set there, but it belongs in objectives
The psychomotor domain: his skill is not yet at the habit level, so more approaches will fix the attitude once flying is automatic
The cognitive domain: he is at the rote level, so drill him on the minimums rules until he can recite every one word for word
No domain: he meets the standard on every approach, and the AIH leaves a pilot's attitudes outside the instructor's objectives
questions.why: The affective domain covers feelings, values, motivations and attitudes, including whether the learner shows a positive attitude toward safety and risk mitigation, and it is more difficult to measure [[25:67|AIH 3-16]]. Training objectives apply to all three domains; standards for the cognitive and psychomotor domains are easily set, but standards for the affective domain are more difficult, and decision-based objectives teach risk management and ADM [[25:108|AIH 5-5]]. His flying already meets the standard, so more approaches or recited rules aim at the wrong domain, and the AIH does not leave attitudes out of the objectives.

questions.q: Your instrument applicant fails his practical test on holding. Back at the school he says, 'I failed because that examiner was out to get me,' and asks you to send him back next week. What does the AIH call this, and what does the retest require?
options: Rationalization; your earlier endorsement still covers him, so the retest needs only a new date, ideally with the same examiner
Denial; refer him to a professional counselor before any more training, since every defense mechanism calls for one
Projection; talk it through to restore his motivation and confidence, give the training he needs, then endorse him and sign a new 8710
Projection; if the examiner caused the failure, he needs no training, so endorse him for the retest today to keep him confident
questions.why: Blaming a poor examiner for a failed flight exam is the AIH's own example of projection [[25:43|AIH 2-10]]. Use common sense and discuss the problem with the learner: the main objective is to restore motivation and self-confidence, and a professional counselor is for severe cases with possible deep psychological problems [[25:45|AIH 2-12]]. A retest needs the necessary training from an authorized instructor who found the applicant proficient to pass, and an endorsement from the instructor who gave it [[60:227|14 CFR 61.49(a)(1)]] [[60:227|14 CFR 61.49(a)(2)]]. AC 61-65K adds that an instructor's recommendation on Form 8710-1 is required for each retest after a Notice of Disapproval [[12:11|AC 61-65K 14.2]]. So neither the old endorsement nor one without training will do.

questions.q: On a practice ILS your learner is well below the glideslope and still descending near decision altitude. You say, 'Take appropriate measures,' and she keeps going. What does the AIH say about your words, and what comes next?
options: Abstraction: say 'Go around,' an action that means the same to you both, and take the controls if she does not respond
Lack of common experience: she has never flown to minimums, so explain how the glideslope works while she continues down
Interference: the intercom distorted your words, so repeat 'take appropriate measures' louder and watch her reaction
Symbol confusion: she took 'measures' to mean measuring the deviation, so define the word clearly for her in the debrief
questions.why: This is the AIH's own example: when an approach is going badly, telling a learner to take appropriate measures might not get the desired action, and it is better to tell the learner to go around, since that action has the same meaning to both [[25:99|AIH 4-6]]. Concrete, specific terms reduce the level of abstraction [[25:99|AIH 4-6]]. When necessary, the instructor takes the controls and calmly announces 'I have the flight controls,' and learners should never be allowed to exceed the instructor's limits [[25:179|AIH 9-9]]. Repeating the same abstract words louder, teaching theory now, or waiting for the debrief all leave the descent going on.

questions.q: In your instrument ground class you teach a departure procedure from a chart printed several years ago. A learner holds up the current chart, which shows a different procedure, and the room goes quiet. Which part of communication did you weaken, and what does the AIH say about it?
options: The receiver: the class lacks the experience to read approach and departure charts, so slow down and define every symbol before going on
The symbols: a chart is only a visual channel, so add an auditory one by reading the old procedure aloud to the whole class
Interference: the message was distorted on the way, so confirm it by watching how learners use it in the next lesson
The source: out-of-date material costs you credibility, so keep a current library; outmoded procedures usually involve rationalization
questions.why: The source, in the AIH model, should speak from accurate, up-to-date and stimulating material, and out-of-date information causes the instructor to lose credibility [[25:95|AIH 4-2]]. It is the flight instructor's responsibility to maintain a current library of information [[25:164|AIH 8-6]], and continued use of outmoded instructional procedures or obsolete certification requirements usually involves rationalization [[25:165|AIH 8-7]]. The learner read the current chart correctly, so the receiver is not the problem, and the message arrived intact: it was simply out of date. More channels for an outdated message only spread the error.

questions.q: Your learner took a weekend ground school on holding from another CFII. Today is her first holding flight with you, and the schedule is tight. Which plan follows the AIH?
options: Skip the ground review, since ground school covered holding, and use the time saved to fly extra holds in the practice area
Brief only the safety items on the ground, then explain the entries in the air while she flies her first hold under the hood
Review holding with her before flight, then brief objectives, standards and safety, and invite questions on any step
Give her the ground school's quiz again; if she passes, go fly, and explain anything she missed in the postflight debrief
questions.why: Even when a learner has had ground school on a task, the instructor should always review that task with the learner before flight [[25:174|AIH 9-4]]. The explanation phase of demonstration-performance happens before the flight lesson: lesson objectives and completion standards, a thorough preflight briefing, appropriate safety procedures, and encouragement to ask about any step not understood [[25:175|AIH 9-5]]. Explaining the entries for the first time in the air moves the explanation phase into the airplane, and a repeated quiz does not replace the review and briefing the AIH calls for.

questions.q: You end every instrument lesson with a short, ungraded wrap-up that tells you what to reinforce next time. After the partial panel and unusual attitude lessons, the syllabus has a stage check with the chief instructor. What are these two assessments, and what do you owe the learner first?
options: Both are formative, so the stage check needs no preparation; it just sets the stage for the next lesson in the syllabus
Formative wrap-ups and a summative stage check; verify she meets the stage's proficiency standards before sending her
Diagnostic wrap-ups and a formative stage check; send her early so the chief instructor can tell you where she stands
Summative wrap-ups and a diagnostic stage check; grade each wrap-up and count it as part of her final course grade
questions.why: Formative assessments are not graded: they wrap up the lesson, set the stage for the next one and tell the instructor what to reinforce. Summative assessments, such as a stage check, measure how well learning has progressed to that point, and diagnostic assessments come before a course of instruction [[25:132|AIH 6-1]]. Teaching instructors should verify that learners meet the proficiency requirements before sending them for any stage check [[25:182|AIH 9-12]], so sending her early to find out where she stands is the wrong order. Approved school syllabi spell out the checks and tests for each stage, details other syllabi may lack [[25:147|AIH 7-3]].

questions.q: In a one-on-one ground lesson you give your instrument learner a problem: the forecast for her planned IFR trip shows icing in the clouds at her filed altitude. She says, 'Just tell me what you would do.' Which response fits the AIH's problem-based methods?
options: Tell her your plan first and have her explain it back, since hearing an expert's answer is the fastest way to build judgment
Save the problem for a ground school class, since collaborative problem-solving works only with a group of learners
Give her a single right answer to defend, so the problem works as a fair test of her judgment that you can grade
Offer limited help, such as a 'what if' question about other altitudes, and let her work toward a solution of her own
questions.why: In collaborative problem-solving the instructor gives the problem and helps only when needed, because learning to solve it without assistance is part of the learning. The method can be modified for one-on-one instruction: the instructor offers limited assistance as the learner solves it, and open-ended 'what if' problems help develop HOTS [[25:121|AIH 5-18]]. A good scenario is not a test, will not have one right answer and does not offer an obvious answer [[25:120|AIH 5-17]], so handing her your plan or one graded answer defeats the purpose.

questions.q: Your instrument ground class arrives for a guided discussion on choosing an IFR alternate, but a scheduling mix-up meant no one got the reading assignment. What does the AIH suggest?
options: Give a brief survey of the topic in the introduction, state the objective, then ask a how or why question
Run it as planned; learners build understanding by sharing what they know, so the reading assignment was optional
Switch to yes or no questions for this class, since learners without background can still answer those quickly
Cancel and reschedule, since a guided discussion can never go ahead unless a prior reading assignment was done
questions.why: Learners normally should not be asked to discuss a subject without some background in it. When the instructor has no chance to assign preliminary work, it is practical and advisable to give a brief general survey of the topic during the introduction, and learners should be kept aware of the lesson objective [[25:118|AIH 5-15]]. Unless learners have some knowledge to exchange, they cannot reach the desired outcomes [[25:117|AIH 5-14]], and lead-off questions should usually begin with how or why [[25:118|AIH 5-15]]. Questions answered by yes or no are the kind the AIH says to avoid [[25:117|AIH 5-14]].

questions.q: In the evaluation phase of a demonstration-performance lesson, three of your learners in a row overshoot the rollout heading at the same point in partial panel compass turns. What does the AIH say this tells you?
options: Each one lacks motor skill, so give all three blocked practice on compass turns until the turns become fully automatic
The evaluation phase is for self-assessment, so ask each learner what went wrong and record whatever each one says
The phase measures your teaching too: several learners faltering at one step calls for a better explanation or another demonstration
The task is beyond their level for now, so remove compass turns from the syllabus as an extraneous block of learning
questions.why: In the evaluation phase learners work independently while the instructor judges the performance against the way it was taught, and from that measurement the instructor determines the effectiveness of the instruction [[25:125|AIH 5-22]]. If several learners falter at the same step, the instructor should recognize the need for a more detailed explanation, another demonstration of the step, or special emphasis in later assessment [[25:133|AIH 6-2]]. Blocked practice gives poorer long-term learning [[25:78|AIH 3-27]], and the evaluation phase is the instructor's judgment of the performance, not a self-assessment.

questions.q: Your school opens a computer learning center where instrument learners work through ground modules while a front-desk aide answers simple questions. You will sign their knowledge test endorsements. What does the AIH say about your role?
options: The aide supervises the center, so the aide is the one responsible for the training and for checking that every module got done
You set procedures that make sure the required training is done, since you certify competency, and you keep monitoring
The software records every score, so once a learner passes each module, no instructor monitoring is needed
Computer modules count only as extra reading, so you must reteach every module in person before endorsing
questions.why: In a learning center with less instructor control, learners are often monitored by an aide, and the responsible instructor needs to establish procedures to make sure the required training is accomplished, since that instructor certifies learner competency at the end of the course [[25:130|AIH 5-27]]. Computer-assisted learning is an add-on instructional aid [[25:130|AIH 5-27]]. The computer has no way of knowing when a learner is having difficulty, and the instructor should continue to monitor and evaluate the learner's progress [[25:122|AIH 5-19]]. The responsibility never shifts to the aide or the software.

questions.q: On a scenario-based IFR trip the destination ceiling starts dropping. Your learner says nothing about it until you ask, 'What will you do if it keeps going down?' Then she picks a good alternate and flies there well. In the debrief she rates her risk management 'Manage-Decide.' What fits the AIH?
options: Accept Manage-Decide, since the final decision was sound and the flight ended safely at a good alternate airport
Discuss it: Manage-Decide means no instructor intervention, and needing your prompt to decide is Explain
Mark it Not observed, since your question made the decision yours, so her risk management was never shown
Rewrite it as 'fair' on a traditional scale, since her own grade is not objective and the record must be
questions.why: On the SRM rubric, Explain means the learner understands the risks but needs to be prompted to identify risks and make decisions; Manage-Decide means the learner gathers the data, weighs the courses of action and decides with no instructor intervention needed [[25:137|AIH 6-6]]. Not observed is only for an event not accomplished or required [[25:137|AIH 6-6]], and her decision was observed. Collaborative assessment is the learner's self-assessment followed by a discussion comparing it with the instructor's assessment [[25:182|AIH 9-12]], as Linda does when Brian rates himself higher than she does [[25:138|AIH 6-7]]. Traditional scales often meet the instructor's needs but not the learner's [[25:182|AIH 9-12]], and forcing the rubric into a traditional grading mold is what the AIH warns against [[25:138|AIH 6-7]].

questions.q: Briefing a partial panel lesson, you ask, 'If the attitude indicator fails in the clouds, should you tell ATC or cover the failed instrument?' Your learner hesitates and answers, 'Both?' What type of question did you ask, and how do you fix it?
options: A toss-up; ask one clear, definite question on one idea, such as how she will tell which instrument failed
A puzzle question; add more conditions, such as wind and altitude, until only one of the two choices is right
A trick question; warn her before each briefing that some of your questions are meant to catch her out
An oversize question; split it into yes or no questions, such as 'Would you tell ATC?', so answers are easy to check
questions.why: 'In an emergency, should you squawk 7700 or pick a landing spot?' is the AIH's example of a toss-up question, one of the types to avoid. Effective questions are brief and concise but clear and definite, and center on only one idea [[25:142|AIH 6-11]]. A puzzle question piles on conditions, and yes or no questions are on the same list of questions to avoid [[25:142|AIH 6-11]]. Closed-ended questions evaluate only the rote level, while open-ended how or why questions draw full answers from the learner's own knowledge [[25:103|AIH 4-10]].

questions.q: Your school runs mock instrument checkrides. Your learner scored best of the eight learners this month, but on one approach she let the needle pass the deviation limit the standards allow. The chief instructor says, 'She's our best; sign her off.' What does the AIH say?
options: Sign her off: she outperformed every other learner, and in the end practical tests rank applicants against each other
Sign her off: examiners sample tasks, so one weak approach is unlikely to come up on her actual practical test
Hold off: practical tests are criterion referenced, so she must meet the complete ACS/PTS standard, not just beat her peers
Hold off two months: the 8710 recommendation is valid only after 60 days of training with no deviations at all
questions.why: Practical tests defined in the ACS/PTS are criterion referenced, because the objective is for all successful applicants to meet the required standards, and since evaluators may cover every task, the instructor should evaluate all tasks before recommending [[25:140|AIH 6-9]]. Criterion-referenced testing grades learners against a measurable standard rather than against each other [[25:210|AIH G-2]]; ranking learners is norm-referenced testing [[25:212|AIH G-4]]. A recommendation requires a demonstration that is in no instance less than the complete procedure in the applicable ACS/PTS [[25:183|AIH 9-13]], and an endorsement for a pilot who does not meet the requirements is a serious deficiency the FAA may hold you accountable for [[25:184|AIH 9-14]]. The 60 days in the AIH is how long the signature is valid, not a waiting period [[25:183|AIH 9-13]].

questions.q: Your instrument stage test has multiple choice items that ask learners to identify chart symbols. You want new items that check whether they can apply what they know, such as picking the best plan when an approach is not available. How does the AIH say to write them?
options: Keep one correct answer and make every other choice clearly wrong, so that only learners who know the material can pick it
Switch to true-false items, since two choices test reasoning better and leave less room for guessing than four
Use six or more choices per item, since extra choices are what raise an item from the rote level to application
Use scenario items where some or all choices are acceptable but one is clearly better, and tell learners to pick the best
questions.why: Items that measure the rote level should have only one correct alternative, with all others clearly incorrect; items that measure a higher level should have some or all alternatives acceptable, one clearly better than the others, and the instructions should direct the learner to select the best alternative [[25:199|AIH B-3]]. Traditional tests usually assess the rote and understanding levels, but carefully crafted scenario questions can assess higher levels [[25:132|AIH 6-1]]. True-false items create the greatest probability of guessing [[25:198|AIH B-2]], and it is usually difficult to write more than four convincing alternatives [[25:199|AIH B-3]].

questions.q: During an IPC the pilot never briefs an approach, and each one goes wrong early: a wrong frequency, then a missed step-down altitude, then a late missed approach. The performance is unsatisfactory. How do you handle the debrief and the logbook?
options: Build the critique around the one glaring deficiency, the missing briefings, with specific fixes, and log the session as dual instruction given
List each error in the order it happened with no comment on causes, then endorse the IPC with a note of the weak areas
Critique only the worst approach to keep it short, and write 'IPC unsatisfactory' in his logbook for the next instructor
Skip the critique to protect his self-esteem, and make no logbook entry at all until he comes back to try again
questions.why: An assessment must be organized, and a glaring deficiency can serve as its core; it must also be specific, so the pilot knows exactly how to improve [[25:134|AIH 6-3]]. Whatever the result of an IPC, give the pilot a comprehensive analysis with suggestions for improving any weak areas [[15:32|AC 61-98E 5.4]] [[15:33|AC 61-98E 5.4]]. The instructor should not endorse an unsatisfactory IPC and should log the session as 'dual instruction given' [[15:33|AC 61-98E 5.4.1]]. Following the sequence of the performance is also an acceptable pattern [[25:134|AIH 6-3]], but endorsing the IPC is not.

questions.q: Midway through the instrument course your learner flies approaches with the needles near half scale and says, 'The standard allows three-quarter scale, so I'm fine.' What do you teach?
options: Agree, and grade every lesson to the test limit from now on, so that he always knows exactly what the examiner will accept
It is a test limit with only a limited margin of safety; set lesson standards that build to or past it, and teach why
Demand centered needles from today on, since establishing standards means using the tightest standard on every lesson
Leave it until the stage check, since standards of performance belong to summative tests, not to daily lessons
questions.why: The ACS/PTS is a testing tool, not a teaching tool: instructors should not focus lessons on the minimum standards for passing the checkride, and lesson completion standards should gradually reach or exceed the ACS/PTS before final checkride preparation [[25:171|AIH 9-1]]. Instructors help pilots understand why they train to standards, how the standards are set, and that meeting the standard provides a limited margin of safety [[25:163|AIH 8-5]]. The CFII PTS states the ¾-scale deflection limit on final approach as its testing standard [[FAA-S-8081-9E:11|PTS Vertical or Lateral Deviation Standard]]. Demanding the final standard at once ignores the word gradually, and training to standards happens in every lesson, not only at stage checks [[25:160|AIH 8-2]].

questions.q: Before your new instrument learner's first lesson under a view-limiting device, he says, 'Once I start hood work, watching for traffic is your job, even when the hood is off.' What do you brief?
options: Agree: on instrument lessons the instructor takes over all of the scanning, so he can keep his eyes inside for the whole flight
Agree, but only on IFR flight plans, since ATC separates IFR traffic and see and avoid is really a habit for VFR training
You watch for traffic while he is under the hood, he scans whenever he can see out, and you brief the control exchange
He must lift the hood every two minutes to scan for traffic himself, so that he keeps the habit while flying the instruments
questions.why: If learners believe the instructor assumes all responsibility for scanning, they do not develop the constant vigilance essential to safety; a learner who enters maneuvers without checking for traffic is corrected at once, and see and avoid is practiced at all times, whether training is under VFR or IFR [[25:181|AIH 9-11]]. For a check flown with a view-limiting device, AC 61-98E makes it the flight instructor's responsibility to remain vigilant to see other aircraft throughout the flight [[15:31|AC 61-98E 5.1.3.1]]. The preflight briefing should also include the procedure for exchanging the flight controls [[25:178|AIH 9-8]].

questions.q: Twenty hours into instrument training your learner says, 'Every lesson is more approaches, and I can't tell how close I am to the checkride.' You have been teaching without a written syllabus. What does the AIH suggest?
options: Explain that progress cannot be judged until the stage check, since only summative tests can show where a learner really stands
Praise every approach from now on so he feels he is moving forward, since frequent praise reduces frustration
Fly more approaches each lesson so he finishes sooner, since his frustration shows the pace is too slow
Use a written syllabus and lesson plans: give a course overview, show his progress, and give notice of the stage check
questions.why: Lesson plans in an organized curriculum help a learner measure progress, and being able to 'see an end in sight' reduces frustration and increases motivation. To keep learners informed, give them an overview of the course, keep them posted on their progress, and give adequate notice of examinations [[25:162|AIH 8-4]]. A syllabus used for recordkeeping keeps both the learner and the instructor informed on the status of training [[25:150|AIH 7-6]]. Praise given too freely becomes valueless [[25:162|AIH 8-4]], and more approaches per lesson leave him just as unable to see where he stands.

questions.q: An instrument pilot who has not flown IFR in a year bought an airplane with a glass panel and GPS navigator brand you have never used. She asks you for transition training and an IPC in it, saying, 'It's GPS, it works like what we trained on.' What fits the guidance?
options: Accept: your instrument ratings on both certificates qualify you, and she can show you the buttons as you go
Accept the training but not the IPC, since only the IPC calls for an instructor who knows the avionics
Decline unless you become proficient first, help her find a qualified instructor, and warn her the formats differ
Accept, and let the autopilot fly the approaches, since an IPC checks the pilot and not her avionics
questions.why: Instrument ratings on both the pilot and the instructor certificate are required to give an IPC [[15:30|AC 61-98E 5.1.1]], but AC 61-98E also says to consider your own qualifications first: if you are not proficient in an aircraft or a specialized field such as transition training in a specific TAA, be honest, decline, and help the pilot find a qualified instructor [[15:19|AC 61-98E 2.4.1]]. A flight instructor needs to be thoroughly familiar with all instruments and avionics used for training, especially given the wide variety of GPS and glass displays [[25:165|AIH 8-7]]. Since formats are not standardized, moving from one manufacturer's equipment to another should give a pilot pause [[25:22|AIH 1-18]], and learning one skill can hinder another [[25:91|AIH 3-40]].

questions.q: A business owner who flies his own airplane IFR to client meetings asks you for an IPC. How should you plan it?
options: Build a plan of action around a realistic client trip to organize the required tasks, and agree on the criteria first
Fly the ACS task table in its printed order on a clear day, since realistic scenarios belong in training lessons, not in checks
Keep the plan to yourself so he cannot rehearse, since an IPC should show how he handles surprises
Script the scenario so he is sure to make an error, since a check is most useful when it uncovers a weakness in the pilot
questions.why: Structure the IPC like a flight review, tailored to the pilot's needs, and develop a plan of action that uses realistic scenarios to organize and sequence the required tasks [[15:30|AC 61-98E 5.1.3]] [[15:31|AC 61-98E 5.1.3.3]]. Before the check, review with the pilot how it will be conducted and the criteria for satisfactory completion [[15:31|AC 61-98E 5.1.4]]. The RMH says IPCs should use scenarios that address the hazards and risks relevant to the pilot, such as one who regularly flies associates to events that cannot be rescheduled [[30:59|RMH A-1]]. A good scenario is not a test and should not promote errors [[25:120|AIH 5-17]].

questions.q: Thunderstorms cancel your learner's partial panel flight. You move the session into the school's AATD but plan to teach from your airplane lesson plan exactly as written. What does the AIH say?
options: Keep it as written: a lesson's unity means one plan fits every place it is taught, from airplane to classroom
Adapt it to the device: practicality fits a plan to its conditions, and the syllabus should flex for weather
Cancel instead: under part 61 the syllabus order is fixed, so weather means the lesson waits for the airplane
Add holds and two approaches, since scope allows far more material in a device than in the training airplane
questions.why: Each lesson should be planned for the conditions under which the training is conducted: plans for an airplane or ground trainer differ from classroom plans, and the instructional aids available shape the plan [[25:152|AIH 7-8]]. A syllabus should be flexible enough to adapt to weather, aircraft availability and scheduling changes without disrupting the teaching process, and under part 61 the order of training can and should be altered to suit the learner [[25:147|AIH 7-3]]. Most instrument rating tasks can be initially taught in an FFS, FTD or ATD [[25:174|AIH 9-4]]. Unity means limited objectives, and scope warns that too much material confuses [[25:152|AIH 7-8]].

questions.q: On a scenario-based cross-country, your learner decides to keep heading toward a real line of building thunderstorms 'to make the meeting.' What does the AIH say about your role?
options: Let it play out, since SBT gives the learner the freedom to make poor decisions and to learn from whatever results they bring
Stay silent and note it for the debrief, since in SBT the instructor is a mentor who does not step in
Stop it before safety is at risk, since her freedom to choose never covers an unsafe decision; then debrief it with her
End the scenario and grade the flight unsatisfactory, since the scenario was a test of her judgment
questions.why: The instructor understands in advance which outcomes are positive and negative and gives the learner freedom to make good and poor decisions without jeopardizing safety [[25:120|AIH 5-17]]. This does not mean the learner should be allowed to make an unsafe decision or commit an unsafe act [[25:144|AIH 6-13]], and learners should never be allowed to exceed the flight instructor's limits [[25:179|AIH 9-9]]. A good scenario is not a test [[25:120|AIH 5-17]], and after a scenario, collaborative assessment starts with the learner's self-assessment and a discussion comparing it with yours [[25:182|AIH 9-12]].

questions.q: Your stage objective for holding reads, 'The learner will explain the three standard entries.' At the stage check you plan to have her fly a hold from an amended clearance and fit it into the rest of the flight. What is wrong?
options: Nothing: an objective names only the topic to be covered, and the instructor picks the level of learning at the check itself
'Explain' is too narrow, so change it to 'have knowledge of holding,' which covers both talking about and flying a hold
The check is wrong, since a stage check may test only the rote and understanding levels, not flying
'Explain' sets the understanding level; write it at the level you will check, with its conditions and criteria
questions.why: Objectives should incorporate the desired level of learning, and phrases such as 'knowledge of' cannot be measured very well [[25:108|AIH 5-5]]. 'Explain' is an understanding-level verb, while application uses verbs such as determine, develop and solve [[25:65|AIH 3-14]], and correlation, fitting an element into other blocks of learning, should be the objective of aviation instruction [[25:66|AIH 3-15]]. Criterion objectives state the behavior, the conditions and the criteria, and test items should measure the behaviors they describe [[25:140|AIH 6-9]], so the objective and the check must match.
